title: GPX Track Distance Calculator: File to Miles
description: Sum the great-circle distance of a GPX track or route with the GPX Track Distance Calculator — read locally, roads not assumed. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a five-point sample track through Manhattan — segments of 1.271, 1.081, 1.147 and 0.756 km — sums to 4.255 km (2.64 miles), each segment a straight great-circle hop between recorded points.
quick_answer: The GPX Track Distance Calculator reads a GPX file locally and sums the great-circle distance between consecutive track and route points, reporting the total in kilometres and miles. Drop the file and read the distance it describes — no roads assumed, no upload, just recorded geometry.

Routes drawn in a planner carry sparse points; the summed chords slightly under-measure curvy paths. Knowing that bias is using the number correctly.

use_cases.title: Comparing two recordings of one ride

body.t: Two devices differ because their point spacing differs: sparse points cut corners, dense points trace them. Same road, honest different sums.
A downloaded trail GPX gets its real length before you commit boots to it — trailhead signage and file geometry often disagree, and feet believe the file at their peril.

Five points from Times Square northeast toward Central Park: segments 1.271 + 1.081 + 1.147 + 0.756 km = 4.255 km total (2.64 mi). Every segment is the haversine hop between neighbours — the calculator's entire method, visible.
A switchbacking trail recorded every 30 seconds can sum 5–10% shorter than the ground truth, because each chord shortcuts its switchbacks. Denser sampling shrinks the lie; it never fully vanishes.

faq: Each track sums separately and a grand total is given — a tour file reports per-day and whole-trip distances together, with segment gaps never bridged.
Why is it shorter than my car's odometer?
Chords cut corners: every curve becomes a straight shortcut. Sparse points cut more. The effect is a few percent on winding roads, negligible on straight ones.
The sum is horizontal (surface) distance. On a sustained 10% grade the true slope distance is only about 0.5% longer — small, and stated so you know which number you hold.
What about gaps when GPS signal dropped?
A signal gap inside a segment becomes one long straight hop between the last and next fix — GPS dropouts in tunnels and canyons therefore under-report in a characteristic straight-line way.
Both are measured; routes are plans with sparse points, so expect their sums to sit slightly under the ridden truth.
A trackpoint every second versus every ten?
Sampling interval changes the sum measurably on curves — the single biggest reason two honest tools report two honest distances.
It can: a stopped device wandering ±10 m stacks small hops into phantom metres. Long stops are why raw sums sometimes beat the route you actually took — filtering drift is a separate step.
